rules.statement: Authenticate a management (control-plane) API request against the tenant that issued the caller's token, the control-plane tenant, and never against a tenant resolved from the request's host or path.
rules.why: Token validation runs against the tenant in the context it is given. A host- or path-resolved tenant may be missing, or may be a workload tenant that did not issue the token, and it changes with the hosting strategy.
rules.check: Look for management endpoints, filters or authorization handlers that build or read the request's tenant/OpenID context from host or path resolution instead of from a control-plane context factory, or that accept workload-tenant tokens.

rules.statement: Open the persistence tenant scope for a tenant-bound management route from the route's tenantId value, not from the protocol-resolved current tenant, and return a not-found problem when the route has no tenantId.
rules.why: The scope then comes out the same under every hosting strategy and does not collide with the resource's own tenantId. The query filter also fails closed, so a handler that forgets to filter still reads only that tenant.
rules.check: Look for tenant-bound management routes that are not nested under a group which opens the ambient tenant scope from the route value, or that take the scope from the resolved request tenant, or that go on without a scope when tenantId is missing.

rules.statement: Use the same route tenantId for both the data scope and the tenant node that authorization evaluates on a management route.
rules.why: When one value drives both, the data scope and the caller's authority cannot diverge.
rules.check: Look for management handlers or authorization requirements that take the authorization node from a different source (body, query, resolved tenant) than the tenant that scopes the data.

rules.statement: Take a tenant-bound resource's owning tenant on create from the route, never from the request body.
rules.why: The route's tenant is the one the caller was authorized at and the one that scopes the data. A tenant ID in the body could create rows in another tenant.
rules.check: Look for create endpoints or DTOs that read a tenantId from the request body and use it to set the new row's owning tenant.

rules.statement: When a management operation runs protocol machinery (token issuance, validation, key use) in the addressed tenant, create that tenant's own context for it instead of reusing the control-plane context that authenticated the request.
rules.why: The control-plane context belongs to the security domain that authenticates the caller. Protocol work for the addressed tenant must run in that tenant's own context.
rules.check: Look for management handlers that pass the request's control-plane context into protocol services meant to act for the route's tenant.

rules.statement: Don't open a tenant scope on management routes that act on unscoped platform, team or tenant rows themselves (tenant list, a tenant row's settings, secrets, keys, owners and admins, current-user and capabilities routes).
rules.why: Those routes act on rows that no tenant query filter covers, and the routes sit on the root group, outside the tenant-scoped group.
rules.check: Look for platform, team or tenant-row routes added under the tenant-scoped group, or an added scope filter on them.

rules.statement: A custom tenant strategy that overrides how the control-plane tenant is named must also override how it is resolved, so the two stay consistent.
rules.why: One member names the control-plane tenant from configuration and the other resolves it. Overriding only one lets them disagree.
rules.check: Look for ITenantStrategy implementations that override only one of the control-plane members (GetControlPlaneTenantId / ResolveControlPlaneTenantAsync).

rules.statement: Name the control-plane tenant ID from configuration alone, without a store read, and probe the shared tenant cache with that ID before any store read. On a miss, materialize the tenant through the same provisioning pipeline that request tenants use.
rules.why: A tenant reached through the management API and through its own address then shares one cache entry and is seeded the same way.
rules.check: Look for control-plane tenant lookups that read the store before checking the cache, or that build the tenant through a separate path instead of the shared request-tenant creation pipeline.
